name: Electric Heaters
hub_intro: With Irish electricity among the priciest in Europe, the wrong electric heater is a money bonfire — but the right one, used to heat the person instead of the whole house, cuts bills. The maths matters: every heater converts electricity to heat at ~100% efficiency, so the differences are in how they deliver it (radiant vs convection vs oil), how well they hold it, and thermostat intelligence. We compare them honestly, running costs included.
guide: All electric heaters are '100% efficient' — read that right

A 2,000 W heater produces 2,000 W of heat whether it costs €30 or €300. What you're paying more for: better thermostats (less wasted run-time), heat retention (oil columns), safety features, and quieter or faster delivery. 'Eco ceramic' marketing changes nothing about the physics.
Match the type to the job

Quick blast in a bathroom: fan heater. All-evening living room warmth: oil-filled radiator (retains heat, cycles less). Heating just yourself at a desk: radiant/halogen pointed at you. Whole-room slow background: panel with timer. Wrong type = higher bills.
The real cost per hour

At ~36c/kWh standard rate: a 2 kW heater flat-out costs ~72c/hour; a 1 kW setting ~36c/hour; a 500 W radiant ~18c/hour. A good thermostat halves effective run-time — that's where savings genuinely live.
Spot heating beats whole-home electric

Electric heating a whole Irish house is brutal on bills. The winning strategy: keep central heating low, spot-heat the occupied room. A 1 kW oil radiator in a home office for 8 hours (~€1.50–2.50 with thermostat cycling) beats firing gas through the whole house.

faqs.q: What's the cheapest electric heater to run in Ireland?
faqs.a: The one with the lowest wattage that does the job, run through a good thermostat. For heating a person: a 400–800 W radiant heater. For a room: an oil-filled radiator on a thermostat cycles off once warm, often averaging half its rated draw across an evening.

faqs.q: How much does a 2kW heater cost per hour in Ireland?
faqs.a: At a typical 36c/kWh: about 72 cents per hour at full power. With a decent thermostat in an average room it cycles on and off, usually averaging 40–60% of that. Smart-meter night rates can drop the cost dramatically for overnight panel use.

faqs.q: Oil-filled radiator or fan heater — which is cheaper?
faqs.a: Same electricity per heat delivered, but they suit different jobs. Fan heaters: instant heat, short bursts, bathrooms. Oil radiators: slow start but keep radiating after cycling off, so they're cheaper across a whole evening in a closed room.

faqs.q: Are 'eco' ceramic heaters really more efficient?
faqs.a: No heater beats another at converting electricity to heat — all are ~100%. Ceramic units heat up fast and some have decent thermostats, but the 'eco' badge is marketing. Buy on thermostat quality, noise and safety, not efficiency claims.

faqs.q: Is it safe to leave an electric heater on overnight?
faqs.a: Only oil-filled radiators with tip-over switches and thermostats are generally considered safe for unattended/overnight use — and even then keep clearance from bedding and curtains. Never leave fan or halogen heaters running unattended, and avoid extension leads with any 2 kW heater.

faqs.q: Can an electric heater heat a whole room?
faqs.a: Yes — allow roughly 100 W per square metre in a typically insulated Irish room (so 1,500 W for a 15 m² room). Poor insulation or high ceilings need more. Close the door: the cheapest upgrade for any heater is a closed door.

faqs.q: Electric heater or heat pump — what about running costs?
faqs.a: A heat pump delivers 3–4 units of heat per unit of electricity, versus 1:1 for any plug-in heater — but costs thousands installed. For heating one room a few hours daily, a plug-in heater is rational; for whole-home daily heating, the heat pump wins long-term.

faqs.q: What size heater for a home office?
faqs.a: A typical 10–12 m² home office needs 1,000–1,200 W to heat fully — but if it's just you at a desk, a 400–800 W radiant panel or under-desk heater warms you for a third of the running cost. Heat the human, not the air.

guide: How do you actually pick the right electric heater for a room?

Answer three questions before comparing wattage or price: how big is the room, how well does it hold heat, and how long will the heater run each time you switch it on. A draughty period-house bedroom with single glazing loses heat far faster than a sealed 2020s apartment with the same floor area, so the same heater behaves completely differently in each. Rooms you occupy for hours — a sitting room in the evening, a home office all day — suit heaters with thermal mass or accurate thermostats that hold a set temperature efficiently. Rooms you pass through briefly — a hallway, a bathroom before a shower — suit fast radiant or fan heat that warms a person, not the air. Getting this match wrong is the single biggest reason Irish households end up with a heater that either never feels warm enough or runs constantly and produces a bill to match.
The feature list that actually matters

Ignore wattage badges and colour options and check four things instead. A proper thermostat — ideally digital, not a vague dial — cycles the element off once the room reaches temperature, which is where most of the real-world saving comes from. A timer or scheduling function lets you avoid heating an empty room before you get home. Tip-over and overheat cut-offs are non-negotiable if the heater will ever run unattended, and matter more in homes with pets, small children or timber floors. Lastly, check the IP rating if the heater might ever be used somewhere damp — a standard heater has no splash protection at all. Everything else, from remote controls to app connectivity, is convenience layered on top of these basics rather than a reason to choose one model over another.
What a 2kW heater really costs, hour by hour

Every resistive electric heater — oil-filled, panel, ceramic, fan — turns essentially 100% of the electricity it draws into heat, so cost is simple arithmetic: kilowatts × hours × unit price. At the current Electric Ireland standard day rate of roughly €0.38 per kWh, a 2kW heater run flat out for one hour costs about €0.76. Run it for a typical evening — say four hours while a thermostat cycles it on and off around 70% of the time — and you are looking at roughly €2.13. Leave it running for a full eight-hour overnight stretch at that duty cycle and the figure climbs past €4. None of this changes with the type of heater; a 2kW oil radiator and a 2kW fan heater cost the same to run at the same wattage. What differs is how much of that hour is spent actually drawing power, which is where thermostat quality and room insulation do the real work.
Electric vs central heating for one room

Firing up a gas or oil boiler to heat an entire house just to warm the one room you're sitting in is usually the more expensive option, especially in older homes with a lower BER rating where a lot of that heat is lost before it reaches you. A single 2kW electric heater running for an evening in one room can genuinely beat the cost of a whole central heating cycle. The comparison flips the other way if you try to heat an entire house electrically: gas and oil remain cheaper per kWh delivered than electric resistive heat once you're warming every room rather than one. The practical rule for most Irish homes is to let central heating handle the whole house at a lower background temperature and use a plug-in electric heater to top up the one room you're actually using, rather than choosing one system exclusively.
Buying in Ireland: retailers, warranty and the energy label

Most electric heaters sold here come from Woodies, Harvey Norman, Currys, Argos, Litely-style discounters or Amazon.ie, and prices for a given model are usually within a few euro across all of them, so it's worth a quick check before buying rather than assuming any one retailer is cheapest. UK-market listings occasionally slip through on Amazon with a UK plug rather than an Irish one — check the plug type in the images, not just the listing text. A CE mark is the baseline for anything sold legally in Ireland; it is not a performance claim. Panel heaters over a certain wattage carry an EU energy label, which is useful for comparing thermostat sophistication between models but says nothing about how a heater suits your specific room. Standard consumer protection gives you a two-year warranty regardless of what a listing advertises separately.

faqs.q: Which type of electric heater is cheapest to run overall?
faqs.a: There's no single winner, because running cost depends on wattage and how long the thermostat keeps the element on, not the heater type. A low-wattage panel or radiant heater aimed at a person for short bursts will usually cost less over a week than a high-wattage convector left cycling all evening, simply because it draws fewer watts for less time. Two heaters of the same wattage cost exactly the same per hour of actual running, whatever the marketing says. The practical answer is to buy the lowest wattage that still makes you comfortable for how you actually use the room, and pair it with an accurate thermostat so it isn't running longer than it needs to.

faqs.q: How much does a 2kW heater cost per hour in Ireland?
faqs.a: At the current standard day rate of around €0.38 per kWh, a 2kW heater running continuously for one hour costs about €0.76. In practice a thermostatically controlled heater rarely runs the full hour once the room is up to temperature — if it's cycling at roughly 60-70% duty, the real hourly cost drops to somewhere between €0.46 and €0.53. On a cheaper night-rate tariff, where rates can fall to €0.15-€0.22 per kWh depending on supplier, the same hour costs €0.30-€0.44, though most evening heater use falls in the day-rate window rather than the overnight one.

faqs.q: Is it safe to leave any electric heater on overnight?
faqs.a: Only if the model has genuine overheat and tip-over protection, and even then most manufacturers and fire safety guidance recommend against leaving any heater running unattended in a room with no one awake to notice a fault. Oil-filled radiators with a sealed element and a proper thermostat are generally considered the safer option for long unattended stretches because there's no exposed heating coil, but 'safer' isn't the same as 'recommended for every night.' If overnight warmth is the goal, a timer that switches the heater off an hour or two after you fall asleep is a more sensible approach than leaving it running until morning.

faqs.q: What size heater do I need for a home office?
faqs.a: For a typical Irish box-room office of 8-10 m² with reasonable insulation, 1000-1500W is usually enough to hold a comfortable working temperature once the room is up to heat, especially if the door stays closed. A poorly insulated period-house room of the same size, or one with a large single-glazed window, often needs the full 2000W to keep pace with heat loss. Because you're sitting still for hours rather than moving around, a heater aimed at you directly — a panel or radiant model near the desk — often feels warmer at a lower wattage than a convector trying to heat the whole room's air.

faqs.q: Do I need a smart plug or timer if the heater doesn't have one built in?
faqs.a: It helps, but it isn't a substitute for a proper built-in thermostat. A smart plug can switch a heater off at a set time or by schedule, which stops you leaving it running in an empty room, but it can't respond to the room actually reaching temperature the way a thermostat does — it just turns the whole heater on or off on a timer, at full output, regardless of how warm the room already is. For real savings, a heater with its own accurate thermostat is doing more useful work than a dumb heater on a smart plug, though combining both gives you the most control.

guide: What actually makes one electric heater cheaper to run than another?

Every plug-in resistive heater converts close to 100% of the electricity it draws into heat, so there's no hidden efficiency to unlock by choosing a fancier model — a 2000W heater always costs more per hour than a 1000W one, full stop. The genuine lever is using fewer watts to achieve the same felt warmth, by aiming heat at a person rather than trying to warm an entire room's air. A low-wattage radiant or PTC ceramic panel pointed at where you're actually sitting can feel as comfortable as a much higher-wattage convector heating air that drifts away and cools before you benefit from it. The second lever is runtime: a sharp, accurate thermostat that cuts the element the moment the set temperature is reached saves more over an evening than any 'eco' branding on the box.
Why 'eco mode' claims mislead

An 'eco' or 'energy saving' setting on most consumer heaters is simply a lower fixed wattage option or a wider thermostat cycling band — it isn't a different kind of electricity, and it doesn't get more heat out of the same watts. If eco mode uses 1000W instead of 2000W, it costs half as much per hour, but it also produces roughly half the heat, so it may take twice as long to reach the same comfort level, largely cancelling the saving. The genuine efficiency gain in heaters worth paying attention to is thermostat precision: a heater that holds within half a degree of your target cycles on and off tightly around that point, whereas a cheap mechanical dial with a wide dead zone lets the room overshoot and undershoot, wasting energy in both directions.
The maths: three heaters, one evening

Take three heaters running for a four-hour evening at the standard day rate of roughly €0.38 per kWh. A 650W mini oil radiator, run close to continuously in a small bedroom, costs about €0.99 for the evening. A 1000W panel heater with a good thermostat, cycling at around 65% duty in a similarly sized room, comes to roughly €0.99 as well, despite the higher wattage, because it spends more of the time switched off. A 2000W fan heater run at full output with no thermostat control for the same four hours costs €3.04 — three times as much, for a room that likely didn't need that much heat to begin with. The lesson isn't that oil radiators beat panel heaters; it's that thermostat behaviour matters as much as headline wattage.
Night rate arbitrage — does it help with heaters?

Not as much as people hope, because comfort heating happens when you're in the room, not on a schedule you can shift to 2am. Storage heaters are designed to bank cheap night-rate electricity as heat and release it through the day, but a plug-in oil radiator or panel heater loses most of its warmth within an hour or two of switching off, so pre-heating overnight and coasting through the evening doesn't work in practice. Night rates on smart-meter tariffs currently run roughly €0.15-€0.22 per kWh against a day rate near €0.38, a genuine saving of over 50%, but it only applies if you're actually using the heater during the night-rate window — typically 11pm-8am in winter — which for most households means early risers rather than evening comfort heating. Some suppliers also offer a dedicated NightSaver meter rather than a smart-meter time-of-use tariff, and the arithmetic is worth checking against your own actual usage pattern before assuming it applies.
Small changes that cut runtime more than any heater spec

Draught-proofing a door and window, closing internal doors so you're only heating one room, and hanging thermal or lined curtains after dark will cut a heater's runtime more than swapping one model for a slightly more efficient one. A heater in a room that's constantly losing warmth through gaps has to run almost continuously regardless of its thermostat quality. SEAI grants don't cover heaters themselves, but they do fund attic and wall insulation and can meaningfully lower your home's BER rating over time, which reduces how hard any heater — or your central heating — has to work to hold a temperature. For a rented room where insulation upgrades aren't an option, a draught excluder and heavy curtains are the closest cheap equivalent, and they cost a fraction of a heater upgrade.

faqs.q: Does night rate electricity make heaters cheaper to run?
faqs.a: Only if you're actually heating the room during the night-rate window, which for most smart-meter tariffs runs from around 11pm to 8am in winter. Night rates currently sit roughly €0.15-€0.22 per kWh against a day rate near €0.38, so a heater running during those hours genuinely costs 50-60% less. The catch is that plug-in heaters don't store heat the way storage heaters do — an oil radiator or panel heater loses most of its warmth within an hour or two of switching off, so you can't pre-heat overnight and expect the saving to carry through an evening you're actually sitting in the room.

faqs.q: Is a 650W heater actually enough to feel warm?
faqs.a: In a small, reasonably draught-free room — a box bedroom, a home office, a section of an open room where you sit close to the heater — 650W of radiant or oil-filled heat can feel genuinely comfortable, because you're warming a person directly rather than a whole volume of air. It won't lift the temperature of a large or draughty room noticeably, and it will take longer to reach a comfortable point than a higher-wattage heater. The honest way to judge it is room size and insulation, not a general rule of thumb, since the same 650W heater performs very differently in a sealed apartment bedroom than in a period-house sitting room with a chimney breast.

faqs.q: Do 'eco' or 'energy saving' heaters really use less electricity?
faqs.a: An eco setting is almost always just a lower wattage option or a wider thermostat cycling range, not a different, more efficient way of generating heat — every resistive electric heater converts close to 100% of its electricity into warmth regardless of branding. Running on eco genuinely uses fewer watts per hour, but it also produces less heat, so it can take longer to reach the same comfort level, which narrows or erases the saving. The feature actually worth paying for is thermostat accuracy: a heater that holds tightly to your set temperature wastes far less energy than one with a loose mechanical dial, eco mode or not.

faqs.q: Which is cheaper — an oil radiator or a fan heater — for the same room?
faqs.a: At the same wattage, they cost exactly the same per hour of actual running, because both are close to 100% efficient at turning electricity into heat. The difference is in runtime: an oil radiator's thermal mass means the element cycles off while the oil keeps radiating warmth, so it often uses less electricity over an evening than a fan heater of the same wattage that has to keep re-firing every time the air cools. For short bursts of heat, a fan heater's instant output can mean less total runtime than waiting for an oil radiator to warm up, so the cheaper option depends on how long you're actually heating for.

faqs.q: Will insulation improvements save more than buying a cheaper heater?
faqs.a: For most Irish homes, yes, and by a wide margin. A cheaper-to-run heater might shave 20-30% off the electricity used for the same comfort level, but draught-proofing a door, adding thermal curtains or improving attic insulation reduces the underlying heat loss the heater is fighting against in the first place, which lowers runtime regardless of which heater you own. SEAI grants specifically fund attic and wall insulation, though not heaters, precisely because insulation delivers a bigger, more permanent reduction in energy use than any single appliance swap. Renters without access to structural upgrades get the most proportional benefit from a cheap draught excluder and heavy curtains.

faqs.q: How much can a good thermostat cut my heating bill?
faqs.a: Owner reports and the underlying physics both point to thermostat quality being one of the biggest single factors in running cost, often bigger than the difference between heater types. A heater with a wide mechanical dead zone might let a room swing several degrees above and below your target before cycling, wasting energy in both directions, while a digital thermostat holding within half a degree cycles the element off promptly once the target is met. The exact saving varies by room and habits, but going from a loose mechanical dial to an accurate digital thermostat commonly cuts runtime, and therefore cost, by a noticeable double-digit percentage over a season.

guide: Why do oil-filled radiators stay warm after the thermostat switches off?

An oil-filled radiator heats a sealed reservoir of thermal oil rather than air or a person directly, and that oil holds heat far longer than the metal casing of a fan or ceramic heater. In practice the thermostat can switch the element off well before the room stops feeling warm, because the oil keeps radiating stored heat for a good while afterwards. The trade-off is a slower start — you feel a fan heater's output within seconds, but an oil radiator can take fifteen to twenty minutes to noticeably warm a room. For anywhere you're settling in for an evening rather than passing through, that slow, steady, even heat is usually the more comfortable and often the cheaper option over the full session, because the element spends less of the evening actually drawing power.
Fin count, wattage, and room coverage

Fin count roughly tracks the surface area available to radiate heat into the room, and wattage tracks how fast the oil itself heats up — the two work together rather than one substituting for the other. A 5-fin radiator around 600-700W suits a small bedroom or box room where you mainly need to take the chill off. A 9 to 11-fin radiator in the 2000-2500W range is the standard choice for an average Irish sitting room or open-plan kitchen-diner, assuming reasonable insulation. More fins at the same wattage generally spread heat more evenly across a room rather than concentrating it near the unit, which matters in rooms where you're sitting some distance away. As with any heater, none of this changes the underlying cost per kWh — it only changes how effectively that energy translates into a comfortable room.
All-evening cost: an oil radiator vs the boiler

A 2kW oil radiator cycling at a realistic 55-65% duty once a room is up to temperature costs somewhere between €0.42 and €0.49 per hour at the standard day rate of roughly €0.38 per kWh — call it €1.80-€2.10 over a four-hour evening. Firing the central heating system to heat the whole house for the same evening, particularly in a home with a lower BER rating where heat escapes through walls, windows and an uninsulated attic, frequently costs more once you account for gas or oil consumed warming rooms nobody's sitting in. The comparison reverses if you try to heat several rooms electrically at once — several oil radiators running simultaneously will usually cost more than one central heating cycle. An oil radiator's real strength is heating the one occupied room for a long stretch without lighting the boiler at all.
Safety for unattended and overnight use

Oil radiators are generally considered among the safer plug-in heater types for longer unattended stretches, because the heating element is fully sealed inside the oil reservoir rather than exposed to the air the way a fan or ceramic element is. That's a meaningful difference, but it isn't a green light to leave any heater running all night without a second thought — manufacturer guidance and fire safety advice still recommend an overheat cut-off and, ideally, a tip-over switch as standard, and a genuine thermostat that holds a safe background temperature rather than running flat out. For bedroom use overnight, a timer that switches the radiator off an hour or so after you're likely asleep is a more sensible approach than relying on it to run unmonitored until morning. If in doubt, treat the manufacturer's stated safety features as a checklist rather than an assumption, since not every budget model includes both protections as standard.
Preheating and timers to smooth the slow start

Because oil radiators are slow to warm up, a built-in or plug-in timer that starts the unit twenty to thirty minutes before you actually need the room is the most effective way to work around their one real weakness. Set it to fire up shortly before you get home from work or before your usual evening routine, and the room is already at temperature rather than making you wait once you're in it. Some owners pair a slower oil radiator, left running for the evening's background heat, with a quick radiant or fan heater used briefly for the first few minutes in a cold room — the fast heater takes the immediate edge off while the oil radiator builds toward the temperature it will then hold efficiently for hours. That combination plays to each heater's strength rather than asking one appliance to do a job it's not well suited to.

faqs.q: Why does my oil radiator take so long to warm the room?
faqs.a: It's the trade-off for the way oil radiators work: the element has to heat the entire sealed reservoir of oil before that heat has properly transferred into the room air, rather than blowing warm air at you immediately the way a fan heater does. Fifteen to twenty minutes before you notice a real difference is normal, longer in a larger or draughtier room. The upside of that slow start is an equally slow cool-down — once the oil is hot, it keeps radiating heat well after the element switches off, which is exactly what makes oil radiators efficient for long evening or overnight use despite the sluggish beginning.

faqs.q: Is it safe to leave an oil-filled radiator on all night?
faqs.a: Oil radiators are generally regarded as one of the safer heater types for overnight use because the element is fully sealed inside the oil rather than exposed, which removes the fire risk of something falling onto an open coil. That said, most safety guidance still recommends against leaving any heater running completely unmonitored, and a model without a genuine overheat cut-off or tip-over switch shouldn't be trusted overnight regardless of type. A practical middle ground is a timer set to switch the radiator off an hour or two after you're likely to be asleep, holding the room at a safe background level rather than running flat out until morning.

faqs.q: Do oil radiators need topping up or maintenance?
faqs.a: No. The oil reservoir is sealed at the factory and isn't designed to be opened, topped up or replaced by the owner — it's rated to last the working life of the radiator. If you notice a genuine oil leak, that's a fault to stop using and dispose of the unit over, not something to top up yourself. Beyond that, the only routine maintenance worth doing is keeping the fins free of dust, which can slightly reduce how effectively they radiate heat into the room, and checking the plug and cable periodically for damage the way you would with any electrical appliance.

faqs.q: How many fins do I need for a living room?
faqs.a: For an average Irish sitting room with reasonable insulation, a 9 to 11-fin radiator in the 2000-2500W range is the standard choice and should comfortably hold a comfortable temperature over an evening. A larger or draughtier room, or one with high ceilings and a lot of glazing, may need more fins or a higher wattage to keep pace with heat loss. More fins at a given wattage tend to spread heat more evenly around the room rather than concentrating it close to the unit, which is worth prioritising if your seating is some distance from where the radiator sits.

faqs.q: Oil radiator vs storage heater — what's the difference?
faqs.a: They sound similar but work very differently. A storage heater is usually wired into the electrical system, deliberately charges up overnight on cheap night-rate electricity, and releases that stored heat gradually through the following day, whether or not you're using the room at that exact moment. A plug-in oil radiator has no such storage capacity in any meaningful sense — it holds heat for an hour or two after switching off, not a full day — and it's controlled on demand rather than pre-programmed around a tariff window. Storage heaters suit predictable daily routines; oil radiators suit heating a room when you actually decide to.

faqs.q: Can I use an oil radiator to preheat a room before I get home?
faqs.a: Yes, and it's one of the better uses for a timer-equipped model, precisely because oil radiators are slow to start. Setting the timer to switch on twenty to thirty minutes before your usual arrival means the room is already comfortable rather than making you wait for the first sluggish quarter-hour once you're actually in it. Once warm, the oil's thermal mass means the radiator doesn't need to run continuously to hold that temperature through the evening, so the cost of the preheat period is largely offset by lower runtime afterwards compared with starting from cold when you walk in.

guide: What kind of room does a panel heater actually work best in?

Panel heaters carry little thermal mass and rely on either convection or a flat infrared element to warm a room steadily rather than in a fast burst, which suits newer builds with a BER rating of B or A, tight window and door seals, and good attic and wall insulation. In that kind of airtight room the heat has nowhere to escape, so a modest wattage running in the background holds a comfortable temperature all evening. A panel heater's slim profile and wall-mounted design make it the closest thing to a fitted heating solution in the plug-in category, but that design is also what defines where it performs. Put the same heater in a draughty older room with single glazing and gaps around the frames and it will cycle almost constantly, trying to keep pace with heat leaking out as fast as it's produced — at which point wattage stops being the limiting factor and insulation becomes the real problem.
Smart scheduling: shifting use, not cost per watt

App-connected panel heaters let you schedule heating around your actual routine, or switch a heater off remotely if you've left it running by mistake, and that's a genuine convenience — but it's worth being clear about what it does and doesn't change. Every kWh still costs the same whether you switch the heater on with an app, a physical dial or a wall timer; a smart panel heater draws no less electricity per hour than a dumb one at the same wattage and thermostat setting. The saving comes entirely from not heating a room nobody's in, whether that's catching a heater left on after you've left for work or geofencing it to start warming up as you head home. If you're already disciplined about switching heaters off, app control adds convenience rather than a new source of savings.
Why panel heaters struggle in older or draughty homes

The same low thermal mass that makes panel heaters responsive and slim also means they have almost nothing in reserve once the element switches off — unlike an oil radiator, there's no stored warmth carrying the room through a thermostat's off cycle. In a well-sealed room that barely matters, because heat loss is slow enough that the panel doesn't need to fire often. In an older Irish home with a lower BER rating, solid walls, and draughts around original windows and doors, that same panel heater ends up cycling on almost as often as it cycles off, chasing heat that's escaping nearly as fast as it's produced. That's not a flaw in the heater — it's a mismatch between a background-heating tool and a room that needs bursts of stronger, more responsive heat, which an oil radiator or fan heater with proper thermal output is usually better suited to.
The maths on background heating

A 750W panel heater cycling at around 50% duty in a well-sealed modern bedroom, held at a steady background temperature over a six-hour evening, costs in the region of €1.43 at the standard day rate of roughly €0.38 per kWh. Move the same heater into a draughtier room where it ends up cycling closer to 85% of the time just to hold the same temperature, and the cost for the same six hours rises to roughly €2.42 — a substantial jump without changing the heater at all, purely down to how well the room holds what it's given. This is the clearest illustration of why panel heaters are sold on room suitability as much as wattage: the number on the box tells you what it can produce, not what it will actually cost you in a specific room.
Installation: wall-mounted vs portable, and safety clearances

Most panel heaters can either be fixed permanently to a wall bracket or left standing on integrated feet, and the choice affects both safety and how well the heater performs. Wall mounting keeps the heater clear of curtains, bedding and furniture, which matters because manufacturer guidance typically calls for a clearance of at least 50cm from anything flammable, more for a heater mounted below a window with curtains nearby. It also lets warm air or radiant heat spread across the room properly rather than being partly blocked by whatever the heater happens to be leaning against on the floor. If you want to use a panel heater in a bathroom, check the IP rating specifically — most standard panel heaters carry no water protection at all and are not rated for a bathroom, even mounted well away from the shower.

faqs.q: Do panel heaters work in older Irish houses?
faqs.a: They'll work, but often less efficiently than in a newer, better-sealed home, because panel heaters have very little thermal mass and rely on the room holding heat well between cycles. In an older house with solid walls, single glazing or draughts around original windows and doors, a panel heater ends up cycling almost constantly to keep pace with heat escaping, which drives up runtime and cost compared with the same heater in a tightly sealed modern room. They're not a bad choice for an older home outright, but an oil radiator's thermal mass or a higher-wattage convector often copes better with that kind of heat loss.

faqs.q: What's the difference between infrared and convector panel heaters?
faqs.a: A convector panel heats the air passing over its element, which then circulates around the room, whereas an infrared panel radiates heat directly to solid objects and people in its path, similarly to how sunlight warms you even on a cold day. Infrared responds faster because it doesn't wait for air to circulate, and it can feel warmer at a given wattage if you're sitting directly in its path, but it does less to raise the overall air temperature of a room. Convector panels are the more common choice for background whole-room warmth; infrared suits a fixed spot like a desk or an armchair.

faqs.q: Can I leave a panel heater running in the background all day?
faqs.a: You can, and it's the use case panel heaters are actually designed around, but the cost adds up over a full day regardless of how low the wattage is. A 750W panel cycling at moderate duty in a well-sealed room might cost somewhere around €4-€5 for a twelve-hour day at the standard day rate — manageable for one occupied room, but worth comparing against simply heating the room for the hours you're actually in it rather than continuously. A basic timer or the heater's own scheduling function is usually a better balance than running it unattended from morning to night.

faqs.q: Do smart or WiFi panel heaters actually save money?
faqs.a: The electricity itself costs the same per kWh whether the heater is controlled by an app, a physical timer or a simple dial — smart features don't make the heating element more efficient. The saving comes from better control: not leaving a heater running in an empty room, scheduling it to start shortly before you're home rather than hours in advance, or switching it off remotely if you forget. If you're already disciplined about turning heaters off, a smart model mainly adds convenience rather than a new source of savings; if you regularly forget to switch heaters off, the app control can pay for the price difference fairly quickly.

faqs.q: Can panel heaters be installed in a bathroom?
faqs.a: Only specific models rated for it. Most standard panel heaters have no IP water-resistance rating at all and are not designed or approved for bathroom use, regardless of how far they're positioned from the shower or bath. If you want panel-style heating in a bathroom, look specifically for a model marketed as bathroom-safe with an IP21 or ideally IP24 rating, and be aware that Irish wiring regulations restrict where electrical appliances and sockets can be positioned relative to water sources — a hardwired, properly zoned installation is usually the safer route for a bathroom rather than a plug-in panel heater.

faqs.q: How much wall clearance does a panel heater need?
faqs.a: Manufacturer guidance commonly calls for a minimum of 50cm clearance from curtains, bedding, furniture or anything else flammable, and more if the heater sits below a window where curtains could brush against it when moved. This isn't a minor formality — panel heaters run hot enough on their front surface to pose a genuine fire risk if fabric is left resting against them for an extended period. Wall-mounting the heater at the recommended height, rather than propping a portable version against furniture, is the more reliable way to guarantee that clearance is maintained day to day.

guide: Why does speed matter more than efficiency for a bathroom heater?

A typical Irish bathroom is small enough in volume that even a modest-wattage heater can raise its temperature quickly — a 2m x 2m bathroom with a 2.4m ceiling is under 10 cubic metres, a fraction of a bedroom or sitting room. The catch is that bathroom heating isn't judged by whether a heater can eventually get the room warm, but by whether it gets there before you're out of the shower and cold. That makes speed of response matter more here than in any other room in the house. A slow-building oil radiator that would be ideal for an evening in the sitting room is the wrong tool here, however small the room is, because you need meaningful warmth within a minute or two, not fifteen to twenty. Radiant elements and fan heaters with PTC ceramic cores lead in this room specifically because they respond fast, not because they're more efficient.
IP ratings and bathroom zones explained

Irish and UK wiring regulations divide a bathroom into zones based on distance from water, and what electrical equipment is permitted in each zone is genuinely restricted, not just a manufacturer suggestion. IP21 is the minimum rating that qualifies a heater as splash-resistant enough for general bathroom use outside the immediate wet zones; IP24 offers stronger protection against splashing water from any direction and is the safer choice if the heater will sit anywhere near the shower or bath. A heater with no IP rating at all is a standard indoor appliance and has no business in a bathroom regardless of how far from the water it's positioned, because bathroom air itself carries far more humidity than a normal room even without direct splashing. Sockets are also restricted by zone, which is part of why many bathroom heaters are designed for pull-cord operation rather than a standard plug.
Recovery time: what 'ninety seconds to warm' really means

Manufacturer figures quoting a rapid warm-up time typically mean the point at which the heater itself reaches full output and starts putting out meaningful heat, not the point at which the room feels warm — those are two different things, and a small, poorly insulated bathroom with a cold tiled floor and no door draught seal can take noticeably longer to feel comfortable even with a heater that reaches full power almost instantly. Radiant and PTC fan heaters win on this measure because there's no thermal mass to bring up to temperature first, unlike an oil-filled radiator's oil reservoir. The practical takeaway is to treat quoted warm-up times as how fast the heater starts working, and expect the room itself to lag a little behind that, more so in an older house with a single-glazed bathroom window or an uninsulated exterior wall.
Running cost for short bursts

Bathroom heaters are typically used in short, sharp bursts rather than running for hours, which changes the maths compared with a sitting room heater. A 2kW heater run for fifteen minutes before and during a shower costs roughly €0.19 at the standard day rate of around €0.38 per kWh — €0.19 x 30 days comes to about €5.70 a month for a daily shower warm-up, a genuinely modest sum even though the wattage itself looks high next to a panel heater's 750-1000W. This is the one heater category in the house where reaching for the higher-wattage, faster-response option rarely costs much extra, because total runtime stays low regardless of how it's used. The maths changes if the heater gets left running well beyond the shower itself, which is where a built-in timer earns its keep.
Wall-mounted vs portable — what's actually allowed

A wall-mounted, hardwired or pull-cord bathroom heater installed by a qualified electrician in line with zone regulations is the more permanent and, in most cases, the safer solution, because it's fixed out of reach of water and doesn't rely on a trailing cable or a socket positioned somewhere it technically shouldn't be. A portable plug-in heater is only appropriate in a bathroom if it carries a genuine IP rating and the room's socket is positioned in a zone where it's actually permitted to be used — check this rather than assuming, since not every bathroom socket is rated for appliance use. For a rented property where a hardwired installation isn't an option, a properly IP-rated portable heater kept well clear of the bath, shower and any splash zone is the realistic compromise, not a substitute for a compliant fixed installation where one is possible.

faqs.q: What IP rating do I need for a bathroom heater?
faqs.a: IP21 is the practical minimum for a heater used anywhere in a bathroom, since it provides basic protection against dripping water and light splashing. IP24 is the safer choice if the heater will be positioned anywhere near the shower or bath, since it protects against splashing from any direction rather than just from above. A heater with no IP rating at all is a standard indoor appliance and isn't designed for bathroom humidity, let alone splashing, regardless of how far it sits from the water source — bathroom air carries enough moisture on its own to be a problem for unrated electronics over time.

faqs.q: Can I plug a heater into a bathroom socket?
faqs.a: Only if both the socket and the heater are positioned and rated appropriately under Irish wiring regulations, which divide bathrooms into zones based on distance from water and restrict what can go in each one. Not every bathroom has a socket at all, and where one exists it's usually positioned specifically to sit outside the restricted zones. Rather than assuming a socket is fine to use, check its position relative to the bath or shower and make sure the heater itself carries an appropriate IP rating — the two need to line up together, not just one or the other.

faqs.q: How quickly should a bathroom heater actually warm the room?
faqs.a: A radiant or PTC ceramic fan heater typically reaches full output within seconds to under a minute, but that's the heater working, not the room feeling warm — a small tiled bathroom with a cold floor and no draught-proofing around the door can still take a few minutes to feel genuinely comfortable even once the heater is at full power. Manufacturer figures describe the heater's own warm-up, so treat quoted times as a starting point rather than a guarantee of how the room itself will feel, particularly in an older house with a single-glazed window or an uninsulated exterior wall in that room.

faqs.q: Is a wall-mounted heater better than a portable one for a bathroom?
faqs.a: In most cases, yes, primarily on safety grounds rather than performance. A fixed, properly zoned wall-mounted or pull-cord heater installed by a qualified electrician is kept clear of water by design and doesn't depend on a trailing cable, a portable unit's own footprint, or a socket that may or may not be correctly positioned for bathroom use. A portable heater can still be a reasonable choice, particularly in a rented property, provided it carries a genuine IP rating and is kept well clear of the bath, shower and any splash zone — but a compliant fixed installation is the more permanent and lower-risk option where it's available.

faqs.q: How much does it cost to run a heater for a 15-minute shower warm-up?
faqs.a: A 2kW heater run for fifteen minutes costs roughly €0.19 at the standard day rate of around €0.38 per kWh — the arithmetic is a quarter of the €0.76 hourly cost. Used daily for a month, that comes to about €5.70, a modest figure given how high the wattage looks on paper, because total runtime stays so low. This is one case where choosing a higher-wattage, faster-response heater over a lower-wattage slow one rarely costs much extra in practice, since the short burst pattern keeps the total electricity used low regardless of the heater's rated output.

faqs.q: Can I use a normal fan heater in the bathroom if I keep it away from the shower?
faqs.a: Distance alone doesn't make an unrated heater safe to use in a bathroom, because the humidity in the air itself, not just direct splashing, is enough to affect electronics that aren't designed for it over time, and Irish wiring regulations govern where electrical appliances can be used in a bathroom regardless of how far from the water they're positioned. A standard fan heater with no IP rating is designed for a dry room and should stay in one. If you want fan-heater style speed in a bathroom, look specifically for a model marketed and IP-rated for bathroom use rather than assuming a normal one is fine as long as it's a few feet from the water.
